title: Zapier CEO: 80% of agent tasks should be done with deterministic code
dek: Wade Foster says 80% of what customers use agents for should actually be done with old-school deterministic code; no code is over, and the new no code is code.
why: A first-hand post-mortem on Zapier betting simultaneously on MCP, agents, SDKs and guardrails, including Automation Bench and concrete internal AI transformation practices.
who: Founders building agent or automation products, engineering leads evaluating model cost-performance, and managers pushing AI adoption inside their companies.
skip: The sponsor read and the closing recommendations can be skipped; the rest is evenly dense with information.

points.h: Knowledge work is moving into people's everyday tools
points.body: Foster walks through his biggest shift in thinking over the past 18 months: most people have already picked a daily AI tool — maybe Cursor, Claude Code or ChatGPT — and that is where the work mainly happens. So getting context and data into that daily tool (an MCP server like Zapier MCP, for instance) is where knowledge work is heading. He splits the market into two camps: one wants to keep people on its own platform building agents, the other, like Salesforce, goes headless and lets you take it wherever you want. He is explicit that the latter is the winning strategy, because that is what tool consumers want and where the growth is.

points.h: The strongest model gets only four in ten automation tasks right
points.body: Zapier's Automation Bench tests models on roughly 600 real knowledge-work tasks, for example ‘just signed the Meridian Core platform contract, mark it as won per the routing policy and hand it to the right team, confirm the account from the account hierarchy table, convert currency if needed, and check whether there are open support escalations’. Foster says the newest strongest model is about 40% accurate, the highest so far, but far more expensive than Gemini 3.7, which creates a curve of ‘how much are you willing to pay for incremental performance’. He stresses the benchmark is nowhere near saturated, and what Zapier wants to prove is that putting Zapier next to an agent produces better output than the model alone.

points.h: 80% of agent tasks should use deterministic code
points.body: Foster's core judgment: the vast majority — his number is 80% — of what customers do with agentic products should actually be done with old-school deterministic code. The approach is to have the agent first decide which steps to write as code (cheaper, more reliable) and only call AI or build agents where reasoning is genuinely needed. He concedes models will keep getting better, but finds it hard to imagine a world where deterministic code is no longer more reliable and cheaper. At the same time he keeps the visual layer: people still need to see what the workflow looks like, to verify ‘is this what I want it to do’, and to use it as documentation.

points.h: The real competitor is the product director who leaves in two years
points.body: Asked what kind of competitor he worries about most, Foster brings up what PG said back at YC: the question then was not ‘what if Anthropic or OpenAI does this’ but ‘what if Google does this’, and what PG wanted to instil was that you rarely fight Google directly — you face a mid-level product director who wants a promotion and will be gone in two years. He says OpenAI and Anthropic are now big companies and will be strongest on models, but they cannot do everything. On the other side, ordinary AI users have actually done nothing and may only have used ChatGPT or Gemini, so most companies are not competing with each other but with ‘do people even know what to do with these tools’.

points.h: Let AI watch you work and find automation opportunities for you
points.body: Foster thinks the hardest part has always been recommendations: what should you do with this thing. This year he started running a workflow where AI looks at his own daily activity in Gmail, Slack, the browser and chats, then tells him ‘you should do this differently’. Most Zapier employees plug their tools into Zapier MCP, run an automation once a week, collect a week of work signals, and get ‘you did this and this, here is a tool suggestion for you to build’. He says half the battle is just getting you to react to a suggestion — the idea does not need to be perfect, 50% good is enough to start brainstorming. He confirms this will very likely be productised.

points.h: The bottleneck in AI transformation shifted from technology to people
points.body: Foster says phase one was AI fluency for everyone, and within a year nearly 100% of employees were using AI daily, so technical adoption was not the bottleneck. After that the question became how to turn individual success into company-level production-grade workflows, and so the challenge looks more and more like a people problem — rewriting job descriptions, rethinking compensation, reorganising teams, retraining people from teams you do not need into teams you do. Brandon, the people officer at the time, was good at this and the team was on the frontier, so he was asked to help the whole company. Foster stresses this is not a claim that ‘the people officer must own AI’: a CMO or CPO could do it too; the point is to see where your bottleneck is and then find the right person.

points.h: Some people burn $30,000 of tokens a month
points.body: Foster says a few individual engineers spend $30,000 a month on tokens, which is an outlier. Zapier currently sets no per-person budget, but has built tools that let people see their own spend and see the cost difference between choosing a strong model and a cheap one across different workflows. When he sees someone spending especially much, his first reaction is to talk: ‘what are you doing, I'm curious’. It turns out some are doing extremely high-output work, while others are using Fable or Astro where it is not needed. He expects token budgets will eventually become a real thing, and that part of AI fluency is some people getting a higher budget because they use it better.

points.h: Using AI is not the problem, low quality is
points.body: Foster says he is not against employees using AI to write communications; the real problem is low-quality communication: people with poor judgment can produce a huge volume of low-quality content extremely fast and drown readers. He offers a few rules: you are responsible for what you send, and the author should spend more time than the reader; you must understand what you send and not be unable to answer when questioned; write requests clearly, saying whether you want a decision, feedback, or just marking it as a draft; verify details, because AI hallucinates and may also pull up a project from three months ago as relevant material, and summaries of summaries passed down the chain turn into misinformation. He also calls out the AI voice — ‘not this, but that’, em dashes, honest truth, load-bearing point.
